stem: A 16-year-old girl has heavy menstrual bleeding and frequent nosebleeds. Her platelet count is normal, bleeding time is prolonged, aPTT is mildly prolonged and ristocetin cofactor activity is reduced. Her father has long had nosebleeds and bled heavily after a dental extraction.
oneliner: 16F + heavy periods + epistaxis + normal platelets + long bleeding time + low ristocetin cofactor + affected father → which protein is deficient?
ask: Deficiency of which protein most likely explains her bleeding?

whyNot.A: Isolated factor VIII deficiency (hemophilia A) is **X-linked** and leaves the **bleeding time and ristocetin cofactor activity normal**
whyNot.B: Factor IX deficiency is **X-linked** with a **normal bleeding time**; she has **mucosal bleeding and a long bleeding time**
whyNot.C: Glanzmann thrombasthenia is **autosomal recessive** (parents usually well) and spares **ristocetin cofactor activity**
whyNot.D: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is **autosomal recessive** with **giant platelets and a low count**; her **count is normal**

answer: Von Willebrand factor (von Willebrand disease, usually autosomal dominant)
why: **Mucocutaneous bleeding** with a **normal platelet count**, a **long bleeding time** and **reduced ristocetin cofactor activity** points to deficient **von Willebrand factor**, which tethers platelets to collagen via GpIb and carries factor VIII. It is the **most common inherited bleeding disorder** and is usually **autosomal dominant**, so a father and daughter can both be affected.

idea.rule: Mucosal bleeding + long bleeding time + normal platelets + low ristocetin cofactor = vWF deficiency.
also: vWF stabilizes factor VIII, so aPTT can be mildly prolonged
Desmopressin treats mild cases by releasing stored vWF
Type 1 (partial deficiency) is the commonest; type 3 is the severe recessive form
The commonest inherited bleeding disorder overall

stem: A 9-month-old girl of Mediterranean descent has pallor and an enlarged spleen. Hemoglobin is low with microcytic red cells and target cells, and electrophoresis shows increased HbF and HbA2, no HbA and no variant hemoglobin. Both parents are healthy. In her red cell precursors, mature beta-globin mRNA is reduced and abnormally long, containing sequence that is normally removed.
oneliner: 9mo F + Mediterranean + microcytic anemia + target cells + raised HbF and HbA2, no HbA + beta-globin mRNA abnormally long → which gene region is mutated?
ask: A single-nucleotide change in which part of the beta-globin gene most likely explains this?

whyNot.A: A promoter mutation lowers **transcription**, but the mRNA made is **normal in length**; hers is **abnormally long**
whyNot.C: Loss of the start codon blocks **translation**; it does not leave **extra sequence** in the mature mRNA
whyNot.D: Loss of the stop codon gives an **elongated protein** from normally processed mRNA, not **retained sequence** in the mRNA
whyNot.E: A codon 6 missense change makes **HbS**; she has **no variant hemoglobin**

answer: Splice-site mutation in the beta-globin gene (chromosome 11)
why: Absent HbA with **raised HbF and HbA2** after the switch from fetal hemoglobin is **beta-thalassemia major**. A point mutation at an **intron splice junction** stops the intron from being removed, so mature mRNA **retains intron sequence**, is unstable and makes little or no beta-globin. The **beta-globin gene is on chromosome 11** and the disease is **autosomal recessive** (carrier parents are healthy).

idea.rule: Beta-thalassemia = mostly point mutations (splice site, promoter) that cut beta-globin output; alpha-thalassemia = mostly deletions.
also: Splice-site mutations give retained introns or cryptic splice sites
Nonsense mutations give beta-zero alleles with no beta chain
Beta-globin lies on chromosome 11; alpha-globin on chromosome 16
